title: How Ryanair Makes Money on £15 Flights

beats.say: Ryanair will sometimes sell you a flight for less than the taxi to the airport. And last year, it made more than two billion euros in profit.

vis.text: Cheaper than the taxi. Billions in profit.

beats.say: That sounds impossible. Fuel isn't cheap. Planes aren't cheap. Pilots definitely aren't cheap. So how does the airline everyone loves to complain about end up as one of the most profitable in the world?
In the year to March twenty twenty six, Ryanair carried over two hundred and eight million passengers, and made two point two six billion euros in profit after tax.

vis.label: profit after tax, year to March 2026

beats.say: Let's break down how. There are five tricks, and the cheap ticket is only the first one.
But first, a bit of history. Ryanair started in Ireland in nineteen eighty four, as a small airline with one tiny plane. It wasn't cheap, and it nearly went bust.
So its bosses looked at an American airline called Southwest, which had found a way to fly cheaply and still make money. Ryanair copied the idea, then pushed it further than anyone had before.

vis.text: Copy the idea. Then push it further.

beats.say: Trick one. The ticket is the bait.
Ryanair's average fare last year was about fifty euros. Some seats go for far less, especially when you book early or fly at odd times.
Those tiny prices are the advert. When a flight to Spain costs less than a takeaway, you don't compare airlines. You just book. And once you've booked, the real selling begins.

And the price isn't fixed. Ryanair's system changes fares constantly. When a flight is selling well, prices climb. When seats are empty, they drop. The fifteen pound seat is usually one of the first few sold, or one of the last ones nobody wanted.
Trick two. Everything else costs extra.
A bag in the hold. A bigger cabin bag. Choosing your seat. Priority boarding. Insurance, car hire, hotels, even scratch cards on board. The airline calls these ancillaries.
Last year, those extras brought in almost five billion euros. That's about twenty four euros from every single passenger, on top of the ticket.

vis.title: Ryanair revenue, FY2026
vis.source: Ryanair FY2026: scheduled revenue €10.56bn, ancillary revenue €4.99bn

beats.say: Think about what that means. If the average fare is around fifty euros, the extras add almost half as much again. For many people, the bag costs more than the seat.

vis.label: extra spent per passenger on top of the ticket

beats.say: And there's a clever psychology to it. You've already said yes to the trip. Adding a bag for a few more pounds feels small. That's exactly why it works.

vis.text: You've already said yes. The rest feels small.

beats.say: Ryanair's boss, Michael O'Leary, has never been shy about it. He once joked publicly about charging passengers to use the toilet. It never happened, but the headlines did exactly what he wanted. Everyone talked about how cheap Ryanair was.

vis.text: Ryanair boss jokes about charging for the toilet
vis.date: It never happened, but everyone heard about cheap flights

beats.say: Trick three. The planes almost never sit still.
A plane on the ground earns nothing. So Ryanair is famous for quick turnarounds. A plane lands, passengers get off, the next lot get on, and it's back in the air, often in about twenty five minutes.
No seat pockets to clean out. Seats that don't recline. Often no air bridge, just stairs at both ends of the plane. Every minute saved means more flights from the same plane in a day.
And the planes are full. Ryanair filled ninety four percent of its seats last year. An empty seat is money thrown away, so prices drop until the plane fills up.
Trick four. Cheaper airports, and very tough deals.
Ryanair often flies to smaller airports, a bit further from the big city. Those airports want the passengers, the jobs and the tourists, so they offer lower fees to get the flights.
And if an airport raises its prices, Ryanair has shown it's willing to cut routes and move its planes somewhere else. That threat gives it a lot of power at the negotiating table.
Trick five. One type of plane, bought in bulk.
Almost the whole fleet is one family of plane, the Boeing seven three seven. That means every pilot can fly every plane, every engineer knows every part, and spare parts are simple.

vis.label: aircraft, nearly all the same Boeing 737 family

beats.say: And because Ryanair orders planes in huge numbers, often when other airlines are struggling and plane makers want sales, it can negotiate big discounts. Cheaper planes mean cheaper seats.
Put all five together and you get a machine. Low fares fill the planes. Full planes sell more extras. Quick turnarounds squeeze in more flights. And cheap planes and airports keep the costs down.

There's even one more trick most people never think about. Fuel is one of an airline's biggest costs, and its price jumps around. So Ryanair agrees fuel prices months in advance, a practice called hedging. When fuel suddenly gets expensive, it's protected for a while, and rivals can get hurt first.
Is it a good deal for you? It can be, if you play by its rules. Pack light. Check in online. Print or download your boarding pass. Skip the extras you don't need.

vis.title: How to win at Ryanair
items: Skip the extras you don't need

beats.say: But if you turn up with a bag that's a few centimetres too big, the cheapest flight of your life can suddenly become one of the most expensive.

vis.text: A few centimetres can cost you more than the flight.

beats.say: So the next time you see a fifteen pound flight, remember: you're not really buying a seat. You're walking into a shop that just happens to fly.

vis.text: You're not buying a seat. You're walking into a shop.
